newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia getting closer to privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Serbia getting closer to privatisation.

text.p: Serbia's Ministry for Economic and Ownership Transformation said on Friday it would conclude a month-long public debate on its draft privatisation law early in May so that the process could start in July.

"Public debate will end on May 6. The ministry will then consider all suggestions made by political parties, trade unions and businesses and submit a final version of the document to the government and the parliament," Serbia's Privatisation Minister Milan Beko told Reuters.
According to the draft document, the government plans to privatise over 4,000 socially-owned companies, involve almost four million people and establish a clear ownership structure.

"The law will give a chance to all public employees to get their share in the economy. Health workers, teachers, bank clerks, policemen, all of them will be able to buy shares in some companies," Beko said.
This did not mean that Serbia will privatise its health or education system at this time, he added.

Beko said the new draft privatisation law did not deal with public transport or other utilities, which will be privatised at some point by a special government programme like many other state-controlled companies and services.

In the case of big state companies like Yugoslavia's only car producer Zastava, whose liabilities exceed their assets, the state will take over part or the entire debt and look for a strategic partner to invest and take part in the management.

"The idea is to liquidate socially-owned capital. We do not expect much capital from privatisation, but we want companies to perform in a market manner," Danijel Cvijeticanin, a member of the government expert team for privatisation, said.
The lingering public debate on the draft law focused on its fairness, transparency and ability to raise enough cash through privatisation to kick-start cash-starved industries.

Despite wide political disagreement over the concept which rejects voucher privatisation and does not tackle restitution, most economists agreed privatisation was a must for the economy which lagged six or seven years behind other transition economies.
Velimir Kostic, former general manager of two scientific institutes now in his seventies, insisted Yugoslavia has lived long enough with an ideology inferior in terms of economy.

"Socialism had lost a battle with the economy. Our economy was under great state and idelogical influence, badly affecting management," Kostic told a meeting of veteran managers sponsored by the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce.

"We must quickly get rid of the legacy of the past. Private ownership is maybe less humane, but this is the last moment to turn to something new. Privatisation is not a magic baton, but offers some chance for the future," he added.

Many critics argued privatisation was not fair because it offered shares to impoverished workers who could hardly make ends meet on their monthly income of around 700 dinars ($124). Some said privatisation was leading to a final big robbery of the nation.

But the first Serbian privatisation minister insisted the government wanted to prevent any cheap sale of shares given away to employees and banned any trade in those shares for two years after they have been acquired.
"In two years we expect the economy to pick up, standards of living to improve and over the period those shares will inevitably retain most of their value," the minister said.
